{{nihongo|'''Mishaguji'''|ミシャグジ}}, also known as '''Misakuji(n)''', '''Mis(h)aguchi''' or '''Mishakuji''' among other variants (see below), is a [[Kami|deity or spirit]], or several, that featured in certain religious rites formerly practiced in the Upper Shrine of Suwa, one of the two shrines that comprise the [[Suwa-taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]] complex in {{ill|Nagano Prefecture|en|Nagano Prefecture|qid=Q127877|lt=Nagano Prefecture|1=Nagano Prefecture}} (historical {{ill|Shinano Province|en|Shinano Province|qid=Q289250|lt=Shinano Province|1=Shinano Province}}). In such ceremonies, the Mishaguji were 'summoned' by one of the shrine's high-Ranking priests, the ''Kan-no-Osa'' (神長, also ''Jinchō'') or ''Jinchōkan'' (神長官), into persons or objects that would act as their vessels (''{{ill|Yorishiro|en|Yorishiro|qid=Q333798|lt=Yorishiro|1=Yorishiro}}'') for the duration of the ritual, being then 'dismissed' upon its Completion.
In addition to playing a role in Suwa Shrine's religious rites, the Mishaguji are also enshrined in 'Mishaguji {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shrines|1=Shinto shrine}}' (御社宮司社 ''Mishaguji-sha'') found throughout the {{ill|Lake Suwa|en|Lake Suwa|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa|1=Lake Suwa}} region and its vicinity. Worship of ''kami'' with similar-sounding names are also attested in various localities throughout east and central Japan. Such deities have been speculated to be related to the Mishaguji.
The exact nature of the Mishaguji is a matter of debate. Medieval documents from the Upper Shrine seem to imply them to be lesser gods or spirits subordinate to the shrine's deity, [[Takeminakata|Suwa Daimyōjin]] (a.k.a. Takeminakata), with post-medieval sources conflating them with Suwa Daimyōjin's children. The term 'Mishaguji' was often interpreted as an epithet of these gods during the early modern period. Outside of Suwa Shrine, the Mishaguji were also worshiped as, [[:en:Kunado-No-Kami|god(s) of boundaries]] and tutelary protectors (''[[Ujigami|ubusunagami]]'') of local communities. In this regard they are functionally similar to the guardian gods known as ''{{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|qid=Q269515|lt=Dōsojin|1=Dōsojin}}'' or ''Sai-no-kami''.
Upon becoming the focus of intense study during the modern period (especially during the {{ill|Post-war|en|Post-war|qid=Q1201472|lt=postwar|1=Post-war}} era), various theories as to the origins and original nature of Mishaguji worship and its relation to Suwa Shrine began to be put forward by local historians and other scholars. One theory, for instance, claims that they were originally deities of fertility or agriculture, another proposes that the Mishaguji were viewed as spirits that inhabited sacred rocks or trees, while yet another claims that 'Mishaguji' originally denoted an impersonal, empowering force in present in nature analogous to the {{ill|Austronesian peoples|en|Austronesian peoples|qid=Q861225|lt=Austronesian|1=Austronesian peoples}} concept of [[:en:Mana (Oceanian mythology)|mana]].
As {{ill|Phallus|en|Phallus|qid=Q168552|lt=phallic|1=Phallus}} stone rods ([[:ja:石棒|石棒]] ''sekibō'') dating from the [[Jōmon period]] and similar prehistoric artifacts are employed as cult objects (''[[shintai]]'') in some Mishaguji-related shrines in Suwa and other areas, a number of authors have speculated that Mishaguji worship may ultimately originate from Jōmon religious beliefs. A few even surmise that the Mishaguji were already being worshiped in Suwa before the cult of Takeminakata - claimed here to be a later import - was introduced into the region; the appearance of the Mishaguji in the Upper Shrine's rites are seen by these scholars to be a relic of original local beliefs. These assumptions, however, have recently come into question.
==Names== Multiple variants of the name 'Mishaguji' exist such as 'Mishaguchi', 'Misaguchi', 'Misaguji', 'Mishakuji', 'Misakuji(n)', or 'Omishaguji'.<ref name="mishaguji no tōsa">{{cite book |author=Imai, Nogiku |editor=Kobuzoku Kenkyūkai |title=Kodai Suwa to Mishaguji saiseitai no kenkyū (古代諏訪とミシャグジ祭政体の研究) |publisher=Ningen-sha |date=2017 |pages=212–281 |chapter=Mishaguji no tōsa shūsei (御社宮司の踏査集成)}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Yamamoto|first1=Kenichi|title=Mishakuji: taiko kara no seimei no tsuranari (ミシャクジ-太古からの生命のつらなり)|journal=Collected Papers on Japanese Culture at Teikyō University (帝京日本文化論集)|date=2010|issue=17|pages=255–271|url=http://ci.nii.ac.jp/naid/40017398675/}}</ref><ref name="Oh">{{cite book|author=Oh, Amana ChungHae|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157-158|date=2011|publisher=Sankeisha|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|pages=156–159}}</ref><ref name="Moriya">Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya Jinchōke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 4.</ref><ref name="Oowa">{{cite book|last1=Ōwa|first1=Iwao|title=Shinano Kodai Shikō (信濃古代史考)|date=1990|publisher=Meicho Shuppan|location=Tokyo|isbn=978-4626013637|pages=212–214}}</ref><ref name="Oowa2">Ōwa (1990). p. 189.</ref><ref name="Miyasaka24">Miyasaka (1987). p. 24.</ref> There are also various ways of {{ill|Ateji|en|Ateji|qid=Q754018|lt=rendering the name|1=Ateji}} in {{ill|Kanji|en|Kanji|qid=Q82772|lt=Kanji|1=Kanji}} such as 御左口神, 御作神, 御社宮神, or 御社宮司, with 御左口神 being the commonly used form in medieval documents penned by the Suwa Shrine priesthood.<ref>{{cite book|author=Hosoda, Kisuke|title=Kenpō Moriya bunsho o yomu: chūsei no shijitsu to rekishi ga mieru (県宝守矢文書を読む―中世の史実と歴史が見える)|date=2003|publisher=Hoozuki Shoseki|pages=55–56}}</ref> Outside Suwa, deities thought to be related to the Mishaguji with names such as '(O)shaguji', '(O)shagoji', '(O)sangūji', 'Sa(n)goji', 'Saguji', 'Shagottsan', 'Shagottan', 'Jogu-san', 'Osangū-san', 'Oshamotsu-{{ill|Japanese honorifics|en|Japanese honorifics|qid=Q35165|lt=sama|1=Japanese honorifics}}', or '{{ill|Shamoji|en|Shamoji|qid=Q1191080|lt=Oshamoji|1=Shamoji}}-sama' - with different ways of writing them in kanji - are found.<ref name="mishaguji no tōsa"/><ref>{{cite book|last1=Yanagita|first1=Kunio|title=Ishigami mondō (石神問答)|date=1910|publisher=Juseidō (聚精堂)|location=Tokyo|pages=2ff|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/993744/20}}</ref>
The name's etymology is uncertain. During the early modern period when the Mishaguji were conflated with the divine children (''mikogami'') of Takeminakata, the god of the Upper Suwa Shrine, the name was explained as being derived from the term ''sakuchi'' (闢地, lit. 'to open up / develop the land'), which in turn was connected with legends that credit Takeminakata's offspring with forming and developing the {{ill|Shinano Province|en|Shinano Province|qid=Q289250|lt=land of Shinano|1=Shinano Province}}.<ref>{{cite book |author=Yamada, Hajime |date=1929 |title=Suwa Daimyōjin (諏訪大明神)|publisher=Shinano Kyōdo Bunka Fukyūkai (信濃郷土文化普及協会)|pages=135–136|series=Shinano Kyōdo Sōsho (信濃郷土叢書), vol. 1}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=Miwa, Iwane |date=1978 |title=Suwa Taisha (諏訪大社)|publisher=Gakuseisha|page=31}}</ref> The name has also been interpreted as deriving from {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|qid=Q269515|lt=''shakujin'' / ''ishigami''|1=Dōsojin}} (石神 'stone deity'), a term used for sacred stones or rocks that were worshiped as repositories (''[[shintai]]'') of ''kami'' (it has been observed that stones or stone items were employed as ''shintai'' in many Mishaguji-related shrines), or ''{{ill|Shaku (unit)|en|Shaku (unit)|qid=Q931805|lt=shakujin|1=Shaku (unit)}}'' (尺神), due to another association with bamboo poles and measuring ropes used in {{ill|surveying|en|surveying|qid=Q816425|lt=land surveying|1=Surveying}} and {{ill|Boundary marker|en|Boundary marker|qid=Q921099|lt=boundary marking|1=Boundary marker}}.<ref name="Miyasaka24" /><ref>Ōwa (1990). pp. 189-191.</ref> The term ''sakujin'' (作神 'harvest / crop deity') has also been suggested as a possible origin.<ref>{{cite book |author=Imai, Nogiku |editor=Kobuzoku Kenkyūkai |title=Kodai Suwa to Mishaguji saiseitai no kenkyū (古代諏訪とミシャグジ祭政体の研究) |publisher=Ningen-sha |date=2017 |pages=181–189 |chapter=Misakujin (御作神)}}</ref> [[:ja:大和岩雄|Ōwa Iwao]] (1990) meanwhile theorized the name to be derived from ''(mi)sakuchi'' (honorific prefix 御 ''mi-'' + 作霊, 咲霊 ''sakuchi''), a spirit (''chi''; cf. '''', ''[[Yamata no Orochi#Etymology|oro-chi]]'', ''[[Mizuchi#Etymology|mizu-chi]]'') that brings forth or opens up (''saku'', cf. 'to bloom', 'to tear open', 'to do/make/cultivate/grow'；cf. also the verb ''sakuru''/''shakuru'' 'to dig/scoop up'<ref>{{cite web|title='sakuru' (さく・る)|url=http://dictionary.goo.ne.jp/jn/87239/meaning/m0u/|website=goo Jisho (goo辞書)}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title='sakuru', 'shakuru' (さく・る、しゃく・る)|url=http://www.weblio.jp/content/%E6%B1%BA%E3%82%8B|website=Weblio Jisho (Weblio辞書)}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tanaka|first1=Atsuko|title=古社叢の「聖地」の構造（3）─諏訪大社の場合 (The Sacred Site Structure of Ancient Shrine Groves (3) Primitive Beliefs in Suwa)|journal=Journal of Kyoto Seika University|page=130|url=http://www.kyoto-seika.ac.jp/researchlab/wp/wp-content/uploads/kiyo/pdf-data/no39/tanaka_atsuko.pdf|date=2011}}</ref>) the latent life force present in the soil or the female womb.<ref>Ōwa (1990). pp. 192-194.</ref><ref>Oh (2011). p. 178.</ref>
==Extent of cult== [[File:ミシャグジの分布.png|thumb|260px|'Mishaguji' shrines by region (in Japanese)]] Research conducted by local historian Imai Nogiku in the 1950s revealed a total of 780 {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=shrine|1=Shinto shrine}}s to the Mishaguji (or similarly-named deities) within Nagano Prefecture, 109 of which are in the Suwa area (comprising the modern municipalities of {{ill|Chino, Nagano|en|Chino, Nagano|qid=Q838660|lt=Chino|1=Chino, Nagano}}, {{ill|Suwa, Nagano|en|Suwa, Nagano|qid=Q846338|lt=Suwa|1=Suwa, Nagano}}, {{ill|Okaya, Nagano|en|Okaya, Nagano|qid=Q838672|lt=Okaya|1=Okaya, Nagano}}, [[:en:Shimosuwa, Nagano|Shimosuwa]], {{ill|Fujimi, Nagano|en|Fujimi, Nagano|qid=Q1204145|lt=Fujimi|1=Fujimi, Nagano}}, and {{ill|Hara, Nagano|en|Hara, Nagano|qid=Q1203041|lt=Hara|1=Hara, Nagano}}).<ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 24.</ref><ref name="Oh164">Oh (2011). p. 164.</ref>
As noted above, worship of possibly related ''kami'' with names such as 'S(h)aguji' or 'S(h)agoji' are also attested in neighboring areas, being notably widespread throughout the {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|qid=Q132480|lt=Kantō|1=Kantō region}} and {{ill|Chūbu region|en|Chūbu region|qid=Q134638|lt=Chūbu region|1=Chūbu region}}s of Japan. Shrines enshrining these gods are found in places such as {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|qid=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka|1=Shizuoka Prefecture}} (233 shrines), {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en|Aichi Prefecture|qid=Q80434|lt=Aichi|1=Aichi Prefecture}} (229 shrines), {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|en|Yamanashi Prefecture|qid=Q132720|lt=Yamanashi|1=Yamanashi Prefecture}} (160 shrines), {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|qid=Q128196|lt=Mie|1=Mie Prefecture}} (140 shrines) and {{ill|Gifu Prefecture|en|Gifu Prefecture|qid=Q131277|lt=Gifu|1=Gifu Prefecture}} (116 shrines).<ref name="Owa199">Ōwa (1990). p. 199.</ref><ref>Tanaka (2011). p. 128.</ref> On the other hand, such shrines are conspicuously absent in the two prefectures of {{ill|Niigata Prefecture|en|Niigata Prefecture|qid=Q132705|lt=Niigata|1=Niigata Prefecture}} and {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|en|Toyama Prefecture|qid=Q132929|lt=Toyama|1=Toyama Prefecture}}, located to the north of Nagano.<ref name="Owa199" />
[[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Mishaguchi-jinja-2.jpg|thumb|left|270px|Ontō Mishaguji Sōsha (御頭御社宮司総社) in {{ill|Chino, Nagano|en|Chino, Nagano|qid=Q838660|lt=Chino|1=Chino, Nagano}}, {{ill|Nagano Prefecture|en|Nagano Prefecture|qid=Q127877|lt=Nagano|1=Nagano Prefecture}}]] The head shrine of the local Mishaguji shrine network in Suwa is the Ontō Mishaguji Sōsha (御頭御社宮司総社) in Chino, situated within the grounds of the Moriya family estate. Before the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}}, the Moriya ([[:ja:守矢氏|守矢氏]]) served in the Upper Suwa Shrine as priests known as ''Kan-no-Osa'' (神長) or ''Jinchōkan'' (神長官). The ''Jinchōkan'' was second only to the ''Ōhōri'' (大祝), the shrine's high priest revered both as the descendant and the living vessel or ''shintai'' of the shrine's deity, Takeminakata, and was responsible for conducting the shrine's religious ceremonies. Summoning and dismissing the Mishaguji in rituals was held to be the prerogative of this priest.<ref>Moriya (1991). pp. 4-5.</ref><ref>Miyasaka. (1987). pp. 25-27.</ref> However, local historians believe that the Maemiya (前宮), one of the Upper Shrine's two sub-shrines and one of the four sites that comprise the Suwa Grand Shrine complex, was the original center of local Mishaguji worship, known as the 'Great Mishaguji' (大御社宮神 ''Ō-Mishaguji'').<ref>{{cite book |author=Kitamura, Minao |editor=Kobuzoku Kenkyūkai |title=Kodai Suwa to Mishaguji saiseitai no kenkyū (古代諏訪とミシャグジ祭政体の研究) |publisher=Ningen-sha |date=2017 |page=105 |chapter="Mishaguji saiseitai"-kō (「ミシャグジ祭政体」考)}}</ref> Medieval records refer to the "twenty Mishaguji of the Maemiya" (前宮廿ノ御社宮神).<ref>{{cite book |author=Kitamura, Minao |editor=Kobuzoku Kenkyūkai |title=Kodai Suwa to Mishaguji saiseitai no kenkyū (古代諏訪とミシャグジ祭政体の研究) |publisher=Ningen-sha |date=2017 |pages=117–118 |chapter="Mishaguji saiseitai"-kō (「ミシャグジ祭政体」考)}}</ref>
==Function==
[[File:Kitazawagawa Daisekibo.jpg|thumb|right|A 2.23-meter stone rod (''sekibō'') from the [[Jōmon period]] known as the 'Great ''Sekibō'' of Kitazawa' ([[:ja:北沢大石棒|北沢大石棒]]) after its place of discovery, the Kitazawa River (北沢川) in the town of {{ill|Sakuho, Nagano|en|Sakuho, Nagano|qid=Q1203700|lt=Sakuho, Nagano|1=Sakuho, Nagano}}. Mishaguji were thought to dwell in various objects (''{{ill|Yorishiro|en|Yorishiro|qid=Q333798|lt=Yorishiro|1=Yorishiro}}''), the ''sekibō'' being one of them.]] Mishaguji are believed to be spirits that [[Shintai|dwell in]] rocks, trees, or bamboo leaves,<ref name="Moriya" /><ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 27.</ref><ref name="Tanigawa193">Tanigawa (1987). p. 185, 193.</ref> as well as various man-made objects such as {{ill|Phallus|en|Phallus|qid=Q168552|lt=phallic|1=Phallus}} stone rods ([[:ja:石棒|石棒]] ''sekibō''),<ref>{{cite book|author1=Louis-Frédéric|title=Japan Encyclopedia|date=2002|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0674017535|page=838|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA838|translator-last=Roth|translator-first=Käthe}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Ouwehand|first1=Cornells|title=Namazu-e and Their Themes: An Interpretative Approach to Some Aspects of Japanese Folk Religion|date=1964|publisher=E. J. Brill|location=Leiden|page=197|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1P4UAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA197}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=''Sekibō'' worship in the Jōmon Period (縄文時代の石棒祭祀 ''Jōmon-jidai no sekibō-saishi'')|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/kikaku/data_files/html_dat/H11_isi/isi0203.htm|website=Suwa City Museum (諏訪市博物館)}}</ref> {{ill|Metate|en|Metate|qid=Q1854307|lt=grinding slabs|1=Metate}} (石皿 ''ishizara'') or [[Mortar and pestle|mortars]] (石臼 ''ishiusu'').<ref name="Owa191">Ōwa (1990). p. 191.</ref><ref name="Oh164">Oh (2011). p. 164.</ref> In addition to the above, Mishaguji are also thought to descend upon straw effigies<ref>Tanigawa (1987). pp. 180-181.</ref> as well as possess human beings, especially during religious rituals.<ref name="Owa191" /><ref name="Tanigawa193" />
This concept of Mishaguji as a possessing spirit are reflected in texts that describe Mishaguji being 'brought down' (降申 ''oroshi-mōsu'', i.e. being summoned into a repository, whether human or object) or 'lifted up' (上申 ''age-mōsu'', i.e. being dismissed from its vessel) by the Moriya ''jinchōkan'', the priest with the exclusive right to call upon Mishaguji in the religious rites of the Suwa Grand Shrine.<ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 26.</ref>
Folk beliefs considered Mishaguji to be associated with {{ill|List of fertility deities|en|List of fertility deities|qid=Q2668203|lt=fertility|1=List of fertility deities}} and {{ill|Vegetation deity|en|Vegetation deity|qid=Q1731105|lt=the harvest|1=Vegetation deity}},<ref name="Oh164" /> as well as healers of diseases like the {{ill|common cold|en|common cold|qid=Q12125|lt=common cold|1=Common cold}} or [[:en:pertussis|pertussis]].<ref name="daijiten802">{{cite book|editor=Fukuta, Ajio|display-editors=etal|title=日本民俗大辞典〈上〉あ〜そ (Nihon Minzoku Daijiten, vol. 1: A - So)|date=1999|publisher=Yoshikawa Kōbunkan|location=Tokyo|isbn=978-4642013321|page=802}}</ref><ref name="Miyasaka25">Miyasaka (1987). p. 25.</ref> Mishaguji have been worshipped as tutelary deities of whole villages (産土神 ''ubusuna-gami'') as well as specific kinship groups (祝神 ''iwai-gami'').<ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 23.</ref> Further reflecting this relationship between Mishaguji and local communities is their being believed to preside over the act of founding villages<ref name="Miyasaka25" /> as well as their being associated with the broadly similar concept of ''{{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|qid=Q269515|lt=saikami|1=Dōsojin}}'' (patrons of boundaries or borders).<ref name="soukou">{{cite conference|editor1-last=Gotō|editor1-first=Sōichirō|title='Tōno Monogatari' kenkyu sōkō (『遠野物語』研究草稿)|date=1996|page=20|institution=Meiji University School of Political Science and Economics}}</ref>
==Mishaguji in Suwa==
Within the Suwa region, {{ill|Syncretism|en|Syncretism|qid=Q172904|lt=Syncretism|1=Syncretism}} with other myths has resulted in the representation of Mishaguji as snakes, as well as their connection with the story of [[Takeminakata|Takeminakata-no-kami]] and Moreya-no-kami; Moreya-no-kami is said to represent the autochthonous worship of Mishaguji that syncretized with the worship of new gods represented by Takeminakata-no-kami.<ref>『東洋神名事典』p. 463</ref>

{{Infobox deity|image=File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Mishaguchi-jinja-2.jpg}} {{Short description|Japanese deity}} [[File:Suwa taisha Kamisha Maemiya , 諏訪大社 上社 前宮 - panoramio (13).jpg|thumb|280px|The ''Maemiya'' (前宮), one of the two shrines that make up the [[Suwa-taisha|Upper Suwa Grand Shrine]] (諏訪大社上社 ''Suwa Taisha Kamisha''), located in {{ill|Chino, Nagano|en|Chino, Nagano|qid=Q838660|lt=Chino|1=Chino, Nagano}}, {{ill|Nagano Prefecture|en|Nagano Prefecture|qid=Q127877|lt=Nagano|1=Nagano Prefecture}}]]
{{nihongo|'''Mishaguji'''|ミシャグジ}}, also known as '''Misakuji(n)''', '''Mis(h)aguchi''' or '''Mishakuji''' among other variants (see below), is a [[Kami|deity or spirit]], or several, that featured in certain religious rites formerly practiced in the Upper Shrine of Suwa, one of the two shrines that comprise the [[Suwa-taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]] complex in {{ill|Nagano Prefecture|en|Nagano Prefecture|qid=Q127877|lt=Nagano Prefecture|1=Nagano Prefecture}} (historical {{ill|Shinano Province|en|Shinano Province|qid=Q289250|lt=Shinano Province|1=Shinano Province}}). In such ceremonies, the Mishaguji were 'summoned' by one of the shrine's high-Ranking priests, the ''Kan-no-Osa'' (神長, also ''Jinchō'') or ''Jinchōkan'' (神長官), into persons or objects that would act as their vessels (''{{ill|Yorishiro|en|Yorishiro|qid=Q333798|lt=Yorishiro|1=Yorishiro}}'') for the duration of the ritual, being then 'dismissed' upon its Completion.
In addition to playing a role in Suwa Shrine's religious rites, the Mishaguji are also enshrined in 'Mishaguji {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shrines|1=Shinto shrine}}' (御社宮司社 ''Mishaguji-sha'') found throughout the {{ill|Lake Suwa|en|Lake Suwa|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa|1=Lake Suwa}} region and its vicinity. Worship of ''kami'' with similar-sounding names are also attested in various localities throughout east and central Japan. Such deities have been speculated to be related to the Mishaguji.
The exact nature of the Mishaguji is a matter of debate. Medieval documents from the Upper Shrine seem to imply them to be lesser gods or spirits subordinate to the shrine's deity, [[Takeminakata|Suwa Daimyōjin]] (a.k.a. Takeminakata), with post-medieval sources conflating them with Suwa Daimyōjin's children. The term 'Mishaguji' was often interpreted as an epithet of these gods during the early modern period. Outside of Suwa Shrine, the Mishaguji were also worshiped as, [[:en:Kunado-No-Kami|god(s) of boundaries]] and tutelary protectors (''[[Ujigami|ubusunagami]]'') of local communities. In this regard they are functionally similar to the guardian gods known as ''{{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|qid=Q269515|lt=Dōsojin|1=Dōsojin}}'' or ''Sai-no-kami''.
Upon becoming the focus of intense study during the modern period (especially during the {{ill|Post-war|en|Post-war|qid=Q1201472|lt=postwar|1=Post-war}} era), various theories as to the origins and original nature of Mishaguji worship and its relation to Suwa Shrine began to be put forward by local historians and other scholars. One theory, for instance, claims that they were originally deities of fertility or agriculture, another proposes that the Mishaguji were viewed as spirits that inhabited sacred rocks or trees, while yet another claims that 'Mishaguji' originally denoted an impersonal, empowering force in present in nature analogous to the {{ill|Austronesian peoples|en|Austronesian peoples|qid=Q861225|lt=Austronesian|1=Austronesian peoples}} concept of [[:en:Mana (Oceanian mythology)|mana]].
As {{ill|Phallus|en|Phallus|qid=Q168552|lt=phallic|1=Phallus}} stone rods ([[:ja:石棒|石棒]] ''sekibō'') dating from the [[Jōmon period]] and similar prehistoric artifacts are employed as cult objects (''[[shintai]]'') in some Mishaguji-related shrines in Suwa and other areas, a number of authors have speculated that Mishaguji worship may ultimately originate from Jōmon religious beliefs. A few even surmise that the Mishaguji were already being worshiped in Suwa before the cult of Takeminakata - claimed here to be a later import - was introduced into the region; the appearance of the Mishaguji in the Upper Shrine's rites are seen by these scholars to be a relic of original local beliefs. These assumptions, however, have recently come into question.
==Names== Multiple variants of the name 'Mishaguji' exist such as 'Mishaguchi', 'Misaguchi', 'Misaguji', 'Mishakuji', 'Misakuji(n)', or 'Omishaguji'.<ref name="mishaguji no tōsa">{{cite book |author=Imai, Nogiku |editor=Kobuzoku Kenkyūkai |title=Kodai Suwa to Mishaguji saiseitai no kenkyū (古代諏訪とミシャグジ祭政体の研究) |publisher=Ningen-sha |date=2017 |pages=212–281 |chapter=Mishaguji no tōsa shūsei (御社宮司の踏査集成)}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Yamamoto|first1=Kenichi|title=Mishakuji: taiko kara no seimei no tsuranari (ミシャクジ-太古からの生命のつらなり)|journal=Collected Papers on Japanese Culture at Teikyō University (帝京日本文化論集)|date=2010|issue=17|pages=255–271|url=http://ci.nii.ac.jp/naid/40017398675/}}</ref><ref name="Oh">{{cite book|author=Oh, Amana ChungHae|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157-158|date=2011|publisher=Sankeisha|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|pages=156–159}}</ref><ref name="Moriya">Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya Jinchōke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). p. 4.</ref><ref name="Oowa">{{cite book|last1=Ōwa|first1=Iwao|title=Shinano Kodai Shikō (信濃古代史考)|date=1990|publisher=Meicho Shuppan|location=Tokyo|isbn=978-4626013637|pages=212–214}}</ref><ref name="Oowa2">Ōwa (1990). p. 189.</ref><ref name="Miyasaka24">Miyasaka (1987). p. 24.</ref> There are also various ways of {{ill|Ateji|en|Ateji|qid=Q754018|lt=rendering the name|1=Ateji}} in {{ill|Kanji|en|Kanji|qid=Q82772|lt=Kanji|1=Kanji}} such as 御左口神, 御作神, 御社宮神, or 御社宮司, with 御左口神 being the commonly used form in medieval documents penned by the Suwa Shrine priesthood.<ref>{{cite book|author=Hosoda, Kisuke|title=Kenpō Moriya bunsho o yomu: chūsei no shijitsu to rekishi ga mieru (県宝守矢文書を読む―中世の史実と歴史が見える)|date=2003|publisher=Hoozuki Shoseki|pages=55–56}}</ref> Outside Suwa, deities thought to be related to the Mishaguji with names such as '(O)shaguji', '(O)shagoji', '(O)sangūji', 'Sa(n)goji', 'Saguji', 'Shagottsan', 'Shagottan', 'Jogu-san', 'Osangū-san', 'Oshamotsu-{{ill|Japanese honorifics|en|Japanese honorifics|qid=Q35165|lt=sama|1=Japanese honorifics}}', or '{{ill|Shamoji|en|Shamoji|qid=Q1191080|lt=Oshamoji|1=Shamoji}}-sama' - with different ways of writing them in kanji - are found.<ref name="mishaguji no tōsa"/><ref>{{cite book|last1=Yanagita|first1=Kunio|title=Ishigami mondō (石神問答)|date=1910|publisher=Juseidō (聚精堂)|location=Tokyo|pages=2ff|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/993744/20}}</ref>
The name's etymology is uncertain. During the early modern period when the Mishaguji were conflated with the divine children (''mikogami'') of Takeminakata, the god of the Upper Suwa Shrine, the name was explained as being derived from the term ''sakuchi'' (闢地, lit. 'to open up / develop the land'), which in turn was connected with legends that credit Takeminakata's offspring with forming and developing the {{ill|Shinano Province|en|Shinano Province|qid=Q289250|lt=land of Shinano|1=Shinano Province}}.<ref>{{cite book |author=Yamada, Hajime |date=1929 |title=Suwa Daimyōjin (諏訪大明神)|publisher=Shinano Kyōdo Bunka Fukyūkai (信濃郷土文化普及協会)|pages=135–136|series=Shinano Kyōdo Sōsho (信濃郷土叢書), vol. 1}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=Miwa, Iwane |date=1978 |title=Suwa Taisha (諏訪大社)|publisher=Gakuseisha|page=31}}</ref> The name has also been interpreted as deriving from {{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|qid=Q269515|lt=''shakujin'' / ''ishigami''|1=Dōsojin}} (石神 'stone deity'), a term used for sacred stones or rocks that were worshiped as repositories (''[[shintai]]'') of ''kami'' (it has been observed that stones or stone items were employed as ''shintai'' in many Mishaguji-related shrines), or ''{{ill|Shaku (unit)|en|Shaku (unit)|qid=Q931805|lt=shakujin|1=Shaku (unit)}}'' (尺神), due to another association with bamboo poles and measuring ropes used in {{ill|surveying|en|surveying|qid=Q816425|lt=land surveying|1=Surveying}} and {{ill|Boundary marker|en|Boundary marker|qid=Q921099|lt=boundary marking|1=Boundary marker}}.<ref name="Miyasaka24" /><ref>Ōwa (1990). pp. 189-191.</ref> The term ''sakujin'' (作神 'harvest / crop deity') has also been suggested as a possible origin.<ref>{{cite book |author=Imai, Nogiku |editor=Kobuzoku Kenkyūkai |title=Kodai Suwa to Mishaguji saiseitai no kenkyū (古代諏訪とミシャグジ祭政体の研究) |publisher=Ningen-sha |date=2017 |pages=181–189 |chapter=Misakujin (御作神)}}</ref> [[:ja:大和岩雄|Ōwa Iwao]] (1990) meanwhile theorized the name to be derived from ''(mi)sakuchi'' (honorific prefix 御 ''mi-'' + 作霊, 咲霊 ''sakuchi''), a spirit (''chi''; cf. '''', ''[[Yamata no Orochi#Etymology|oro-chi]]'', ''[[Mizuchi#Etymology|mizu-chi]]'') that brings forth or opens up (''saku'', cf. 'to bloom', 'to tear open', 'to do/make/cultivate/grow'；cf. also the verb ''sakuru''/''shakuru'' 'to dig/scoop up'<ref>{{cite web|title='sakuru' (さく・る)|url=http://dictionary.goo.ne.jp/jn/87239/meaning/m0u/|website=goo Jisho (goo辞書)}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title='sakuru', 'shakuru' (さく・る、しゃく・る)|url=http://www.weblio.jp/content/%E6%B1%BA%E3%82%8B|website=Weblio Jisho (Weblio辞書)}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tanaka|first1=Atsuko|title=古社叢の「聖地」の構造（3）─諏訪大社の場合 (The Sacred Site Structure of Ancient Shrine Groves (3) Primitive Beliefs in Suwa)|journal=Journal of Kyoto Seika University|page=130|url=http://www.kyoto-seika.ac.jp/researchlab/wp/wp-content/uploads/kiyo/pdf-data/no39/tanaka_atsuko.pdf|date=2011}}</ref>) the latent life force present in the soil or the female womb.<ref>Ōwa (1990). pp. 192-194.</ref><ref>Oh (2011). p. 178.</ref>
==Extent of cult== [[File:ミシャグジの分布.png|thumb|260px|'Mishaguji' shrines by region (in Japanese)]] Research conducted by local historian Imai Nogiku in the 1950s revealed a total of 780 {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=shrine|1=Shinto shrine}}s to the Mishaguji (or similarly-named deities) within Nagano Prefecture, 109 of which are in the Suwa area (comprising the modern municipalities of {{ill|Chino, Nagano|en|Chino, Nagano|qid=Q838660|lt=Chino|1=Chino, Nagano}}, {{ill|Suwa, Nagano|en|Suwa, Nagano|qid=Q846338|lt=Suwa|1=Suwa, Nagano}}, {{ill|Okaya, Nagano|en|Okaya, Nagano|qid=Q838672|lt=Okaya|1=Okaya, Nagano}}, [[:en:Shimosuwa, Nagano|Shimosuwa]], {{ill|Fujimi, Nagano|en|Fujimi, Nagano|qid=Q1204145|lt=Fujimi|1=Fujimi, Nagano}}, and {{ill|Hara, Nagano|en|Hara, Nagano|qid=Q1203041|lt=Hara|1=Hara, Nagano}}).<ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 24.</ref><ref name="Oh164">Oh (2011). p. 164.</ref>
As noted above, worship of possibly related ''kami'' with names such as 'S(h)aguji' or 'S(h)agoji' are also attested in neighboring areas, being notably widespread throughout the {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|qid=Q132480|lt=Kantō|1=Kantō region}} and {{ill|Chūbu region|en|Chūbu region|qid=Q134638|lt=Chūbu region|1=Chūbu region}}s of Japan. Shrines enshrining these gods are found in places such as {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|qid=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka|1=Shizuoka Prefecture}} (233 shrines), {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en|Aichi Prefecture|qid=Q80434|lt=Aichi|1=Aichi Prefecture}} (229 shrines), {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|en|Yamanashi Prefecture|qid=Q132720|lt=Yamanashi|1=Yamanashi Prefecture}} (160 shrines), {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|qid=Q128196|lt=Mie|1=Mie Prefecture}} (140 shrines) and {{ill|Gifu Prefecture|en|Gifu Prefecture|qid=Q131277|lt=Gifu|1=Gifu Prefecture}} (116 shrines).<ref name="Owa199">Ōwa (1990). p. 199.</ref><ref>Tanaka (2011). p. 128.</ref> On the other hand, such shrines are conspicuously absent in the two prefectures of {{ill|Niigata Prefecture|en|Niigata Prefecture|qid=Q132705|lt=Niigata|1=Niigata Prefecture}} and {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|en|Toyama Prefecture|qid=Q132929|lt=Toyama|1=Toyama Prefecture}}, located to the north of Nagano.<ref name="Owa199" />
[[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Mishaguchi-jinja-2.jpg|thumb|left|270px|Ontō Mishaguji Sōsha (御頭御社宮司総社) in {{ill|Chino, Nagano|en|Chino, Nagano|qid=Q838660|lt=Chino|1=Chino, Nagano}}, {{ill|Nagano Prefecture|en|Nagano Prefecture|qid=Q127877|lt=Nagano|1=Nagano Prefecture}}]] The head shrine of the local Mishaguji shrine network in Suwa is the Ontō Mishaguji Sōsha (御頭御社宮司総社) in Chino, situated within the grounds of the Moriya family estate. Before the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}}, the Moriya ([[:ja:守矢氏|守矢氏]]) served in the Upper Suwa Shrine as priests known as ''Kan-no-Osa'' (神長) or ''Jinchōkan'' (神長官). The ''Jinchōkan'' was second only to the ''Ōhōri'' (大祝), the shrine's high priest revered both as the descendant and the living vessel or ''shintai'' of the shrine's deity, Takeminakata, and was responsible for conducting the shrine's religious ceremonies. Summoning and dismissing the Mishaguji in rituals was held to be the prerogative of this priest.<ref>Moriya (1991). pp. 4-5.</ref><ref>Miyasaka. (1987). pp. 25-27.</ref> However, local historians believe that the Maemiya (前宮), one of the Upper Shrine's two sub-shrines and one of the four sites that comprise the Suwa Grand Shrine complex, was the original center of local Mishaguji worship, known as the 'Great Mishaguji' (大御社宮神 ''Ō-Mishaguji'').<ref>{{cite book |author=Kitamura, Minao |editor=Kobuzoku Kenkyūkai |title=Kodai Suwa to Mishaguji saiseitai no kenkyū (古代諏訪とミシャグジ祭政体の研究) |publisher=Ningen-sha |date=2017 |page=105 |chapter="Mishaguji saiseitai"-kō (「ミシャグジ祭政体」考)}}</ref> Medieval records refer to the "twenty Mishaguji of the Maemiya" (前宮廿ノ御社宮神).<ref>{{cite book |author=Kitamura, Minao |editor=Kobuzoku Kenkyūkai |title=Kodai Suwa to Mishaguji saiseitai no kenkyū (古代諏訪とミシャグジ祭政体の研究) |publisher=Ningen-sha |date=2017 |pages=117–118 |chapter="Mishaguji saiseitai"-kō (「ミシャグジ祭政体」考)}}</ref>
==Function==
[[File:Kitazawagawa Daisekibo.jpg|thumb|right|A 2.23-meter stone rod (''sekibō'') from the [[Jōmon period]] known as the 'Great ''Sekibō'' of Kitazawa' ([[:ja:北沢大石棒|北沢大石棒]]) after its place of discovery, the Kitazawa River (北沢川) in the town of {{ill|Sakuho, Nagano|en|Sakuho, Nagano|qid=Q1203700|lt=Sakuho, Nagano|1=Sakuho, Nagano}}. Mishaguji were thought to dwell in various objects (''{{ill|Yorishiro|en|Yorishiro|qid=Q333798|lt=Yorishiro|1=Yorishiro}}''), the ''sekibō'' being one of them.]] Mishaguji are believed to be spirits that [[Shintai|dwell in]] rocks, trees, or bamboo leaves,<ref name="Moriya" /><ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 27.</ref><ref name="Tanigawa193">Tanigawa (1987). p. 185, 193.</ref> as well as various man-made objects such as {{ill|Phallus|en|Phallus|qid=Q168552|lt=phallic|1=Phallus}} stone rods ([[:ja:石棒|石棒]] ''sekibō''),<ref>{{cite book|author1=Louis-Frédéric|title=Japan Encyclopedia|date=2002|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0674017535|page=838|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA838|translator-last=Roth|translator-first=Käthe}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Ouwehand|first1=Cornells|title=Namazu-e and Their Themes: An Interpretative Approach to Some Aspects of Japanese Folk Religion|date=1964|publisher=E. J. Brill|location=Leiden|page=197|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1P4UAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA197}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=''Sekibō'' worship in the Jōmon Period (縄文時代の石棒祭祀 ''Jōmon-jidai no sekibō-saishi'')|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/kikaku/data_files/html_dat/H11_isi/isi0203.htm|website=Suwa City Museum (諏訪市博物館)}}</ref> {{ill|Metate|en|Metate|qid=Q1854307|lt=grinding slabs|1=Metate}} (石皿 ''ishizara'') or [[Mortar and pestle|mortars]] (石臼 ''ishiusu'').<ref name="Owa191">Ōwa (1990). p. 191.</ref><ref name="Oh164">Oh (2011). p. 164.</ref> In addition to the above, Mishaguji are also thought to descend upon straw effigies<ref>Tanigawa (1987). pp. 180-181.</ref> as well as possess human beings, especially during religious rituals.<ref name="Owa191" /><ref name="Tanigawa193" />
This concept of Mishaguji as a possessing spirit are reflected in texts that describe Mishaguji being 'brought down' (降申 ''oroshi-mōsu'', i.e. being summoned into a repository, whether human or object) or 'lifted up' (上申 ''age-mōsu'', i.e. being dismissed from its vessel) by the Moriya ''jinchōkan'', the priest with the exclusive right to call upon Mishaguji in the religious rites of the Suwa Grand Shrine.<ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 26.</ref>
Folk beliefs considered Mishaguji to be associated with {{ill|List of fertility deities|en|List of fertility deities|qid=Q2668203|lt=fertility|1=List of fertility deities}} and {{ill|Vegetation deity|en|Vegetation deity|qid=Q1731105|lt=the harvest|1=Vegetation deity}},<ref name="Oh164" /> as well as healers of diseases like the {{ill|common cold|en|common cold|qid=Q12125|lt=common cold|1=Common cold}} or [[:en:pertussis|pertussis]].<ref name="daijiten802">{{cite book|editor=Fukuta, Ajio|display-editors=etal|title=日本民俗大辞典〈上〉あ〜そ (Nihon Minzoku Daijiten, vol. 1: A - So)|date=1999|publisher=Yoshikawa Kōbunkan|location=Tokyo|isbn=978-4642013321|page=802}}</ref><ref name="Miyasaka25">Miyasaka (1987). p. 25.</ref> Mishaguji have been worshipped as tutelary deities of whole villages (産土神 ''ubusuna-gami'') as well as specific kinship groups (祝神 ''iwai-gami'').<ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 23.</ref> Further reflecting this relationship between Mishaguji and local communities is their being believed to preside over the act of founding villages<ref name="Miyasaka25" /> as well as their being associated with the broadly similar concept of ''{{ill|Dōsojin|en|Dōsojin|qid=Q269515|lt=saikami|1=Dōsojin}}'' (patrons of boundaries or borders).<ref name="soukou">{{cite conference|editor1-last=Gotō|editor1-first=Sōichirō|title='Tōno Monogatari' kenkyu sōkō (『遠野物語』研究草稿)|date=1996|page=20|institution=Meiji University School of Political Science and Economics}}</ref>
==Mishaguji in Suwa==
Within the Suwa region, {{ill|Syncretism|en|Syncretism|qid=Q172904|lt=Syncretism|1=Syncretism}} with other myths has resulted in the representation of Mishaguji as snakes, as well as their connection with the story of [[Takeminakata|Takeminakata-no-kami]] and Moreya-no-kami; Moreya-no-kami is said to represent the autochthonous worship of Mishaguji that syncretized with the worship of new gods represented by Takeminakata-no-kami.<ref>『東洋神名事典』p. 463</ref>
